definition: Any person; used in questions, negative statements, and conditional sentences to refer to an unspecified person.
examples: ["Is anybody home?", "I didn't see anybody I knew at the party."]
usage_notes: "Anybody" and "anyone" are interchangeable, but "anybody" is slightly more informal. It is grammatically singular, so it takes a singular verb (e.g., "Does anybody know?"), but is often referred to with plural pronouns (e.g., "Does anybody have their keys?").

definition: Any person; used in questions, negative statements, and conditional sentences, or to mean 'any person at all' in positive sentences.
examples: ["Does anyone know where the library is?", "Anyone can join the club, regardless of their age."]
usage_notes: Written as one word. Do not confuse with 'any one' (two words), which refers to one specific person or thing from a group.
collocations: ["anyone else", "hardly anyone", "is anyone there", "anyone who wants"]

definition: Used to refer to a thing, no matter what kind, especially in questions, negative statements, or conditional sentences.
examples: ["Is there anything I can do to help you?", "I haven't eaten anything since breakfast."]
usage_notes: Use 'anything' in questions and negative sentences, but use 'something' in positive statements. 'Anything' can also mean 'it doesn't matter which thing' in positive sentences (e.g., 'You can choose anything you want').
collocations: ["anything else", "hardly anything", "do anything", "if anything", "anything at all"]

definition: Used to change the subject, return to an earlier topic, or to indicate that something is true despite other facts.
examples: ["It was raining, but we went for a walk anyway.", "Anyway, as I was saying before we were interrupted, the meeting is at two o'clock."]
usage_notes: Often used as a transition word in spoken English. Be careful not to confuse it with 'anyways', which is considered informal or non-standard.

definition: In, at, or to any place. It is often used in questions, negative statements, or to mean 'it doesn't matter where'.
examples: ["I can't find my keys anywhere in the house.", "You can sit anywhere you like."]
usage_notes: 'Anywhere' is a single word. Avoid writing it as 'any where'. In British English, 'anyplace' is sometimes used informally, but 'anywhere' is standard in all dialects.

definition: Separated by a distance in time, space, or relation; not together.
examples: ["The two houses were built about fifty yards apart.", "We had to take the old clock apart to see what was wrong with it."]
usage_notes: Often used with 'from' (e.g., 'apart from') to mean 'except for' or 'in addition to'. It is also commonly paired with verbs like 'take' (take apart) and 'fall' (fall apart).

definition: Except for, or in addition to; used to show that someone or something is not included in a statement, or to introduce an extra point.
examples: ["Apart from a few minor spelling mistakes, your essay was excellent.", "Apart from the high price, the hotel was absolutely perfect."]
usage_notes: This phrase can mean both 'excluding' (except for) and 'including' (in addition to), depending on the context. It is synonymous with 'aside from' in American English.
collocations: ["apart from that", "apart from the fact that", "apart from anything else", "apart from a few"]

definition: A set of rooms for living in, usually on one floor of a building containing other similar sets of rooms.
examples: ["She lives in a modern two-bedroom apartment in the city center.", "They are looking to rent a cheap apartment near the university."]
usage_notes: In British English, the word 'flat' is much more commonly used instead of 'apartment'.
collocations: ["rent an apartment", "studio apartment", "apartment building", "spacious apartment", "furnished apartment"]

definition: To say that you are sorry for doing something wrong or causing a problem.
examples: ["I want to apologize for being late to the meeting.", "She apologized to her friend after they had an argument."]
usage_notes: Commonly used with the preposition 'to' for the person being addressed (apologize to someone) and 'for' for the reason (apologize for something). In British English, it is often spelled 'apologise'.
collocations: ["apologize sincerely", "apologize for the delay", "apologize to someone", "publicly apologize", "demand an apology"]

definition: Easy to see or understand, or seeming to be true although it may not actually be so.
examples: ["It became apparent that she was not going to change her mind.", "Their apparent success was actually the result of a lot of hidden debt."]
usage_notes: Often used before a noun to mean 'seeming' (e.g., 'his apparent wealth'), or after a verb like 'become' or 'be' to mean 'obvious' (e.g., 'it is apparent that...').
collocations: ["become apparent", "for no apparent reason", "apparent discrepancy", "heir apparent", "apparent ease"]

definition: Used to say that something seems to be true based on what you have heard, read, or seen, even though you are not completely sure.
examples: ["Apparently, the meeting has been postponed until next Thursday.", "I thought they were married, but apparently they are just good friends."]
usage_notes: It is often placed at the beginning of a sentence to introduce a piece of information you learned from someone else. It can sound slightly informal or conversational, but it is also common in written English.

definition: To make a serious, urgent, or formal request for help, mercy, or a change in a decision; or to be attractive and interesting to someone.
examples: ["The charity made an urgent appeal for donations to help the flood victims.", "The idea of working from home doesn't appeal to everyone."]
usage_notes: When meaning 'to be attractive,' it is followed by the preposition 'to' (e.g., 'it appeals to me'). In legal contexts, it can be used as a verb or a noun to describe challenging a court decision.
collocations: ["appeal to someone", "make an appeal", "lose its appeal", "broad appeal", "lodge an appeal"]

definition: To start to be seen, or to give the impression of being or doing something.
examples: ["A small boat suddenly appeared on the horizon.", "She tried to appear calm, but she was actually very nervous."]
usage_notes: Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., 'He appears to be lost') or a 'that' clause. In the sense of 'to seem', it is a linking verb and is followed by an adjective, not an adverb.
collocations: ["appear to be", "suddenly appear", "appear in public", "make an appearance"]

definition: The way that someone or something looks on the outside, or the act of coming into sight or public view.
examples: ["She was very professional in her dress and general appearance.", "The famous author made a brief appearance at the local bookstore."]
usage_notes: The word can refer to physical looks (countable or uncountable) or the act of showing up (countable). Common verbs used with it include 'keep up' (to maintain a good social image) and 'make' (to show up).
collocations: ["physical appearance", "make an appearance", "personal appearance", "keep up appearances", "sudden appearance"]

definition: A round fruit with red, green, or yellow skin and crisp white flesh.

usage_notes: Countable noun. Often used in common idioms like 'the apple of my eye' (someone highly cherished) or 'an apple a day keeps the doctor away'.
collocations: ["apple pie", "bite an apple", "rotten apple", "apple juice", "crisp apple"]

definition: A formal request for something such as a job, position, or permission, or a computer program designed for a specific purpose.

definition: To make a formal request for something, such as a job or admission to a school; or to put something into use or action.

definition: A formal agreement to meet someone at a specific time and place, usually for business or medical reasons.

definition: To recognize the full value of something, or to be grateful for something someone has done.
